steps.text: **The question of this lesson.** The Martian Gambit gives away a whole knight on move seven and takes nothing back at once. Why would anyone play it, what does the knight attack on e6, and what does each side have afterwards? By the end you can answer in your own words. Marks: [V] checked here, [S] one source, [R] recalled, [I] inference, [H] guess.

steps.text: **Why a second gambit.** [S] Volen Dyulgerov (CM, online name Witty_Alien) popularised the Alien Gambit, where White sacrifices a knight on f7 after 4...Nf6. Same first moves, different fourth move for Black.

steps.chapter: After 8.Ne5: what White is paying for

steps.text: **What White hopes to buy.** Three ideas, all my readings [I]. **Time:** Black's bishop must move again while the other kingside pieces stay at home. **Light squares:** with the f7 pawn gone, e6, f7 and g6 are easy targets for a light-squared bishop. **The king:** it has lost its f-pawn and faces a half-open file. The boards and the engine are the checks, not these sentences.

steps.caption: Count Black's kingside after 8.Ne5. The bishop on f8 is shut in by its own pawns on e7 and g7 and has no move. The knight on g8 has one square, f6, and the rook on h8 one square, h7. Black has an extra knight, but three pieces cannot yet join the game.

line.say: White develops with a threat; look at how little room Black's kingside has.

claims.statement: The bishop on f8 has no legal move.
The knight on g8 has one legal move.

steps.caption: A map of the pawns. After the capture, Black's pawns on e6 and e7 have no neighbours: they are isolated. The squares e4, e5 and g6 are holes: no black pawn can guard them by advancing. White's knight on e5 sits on one, protected by the d4 pawn. [I] This is why the knight is hard to remove and why the bishop has no safe pawn-protected square on g6.

steps.text: **Credit and honesty.** [S] The line is named for Volen Dyulgerov (CM, online name Witty_Alien), who popularised it. [S-video] In a February 2025 stream he says he invented it in July 2024; the first Martian video on his channel is dated 11 July 2024 [V]. Who played it first is not settled [I]. His win rates have no sample sizes, so this course never uses them.

steps.caption: What people actually do. [V] Online (Lichess, September 2026; a random sample of that month's rated blitz, rapid and classical games, 4,752,291 of them): of the 113 games that reached ...h6, White played 7.Ne6 in 53, 7.Nh3 in 30 and 7.Nxf7 in 21.

steps.text: **How White scored.** [V] After 7.Ne6, White scored 75.5% over 53 games (wins plus half the draws): below 1500, 87.5% over 8; 1500 to 1900, 71.0% over 31; 1900 and up, 78.6% over 14. After 7...fxe6 8.Ne5, 69.8% over 43. [H] The samples are tiny, and players who choose a gambit may have studied it. Online amateur data is not master theory.

fields.label: What the knight attacks and why Black must take:

steps.text: **Recap.** A quiet retreat is the engine's choice, but the gambit gives the knight anyway. On e6 it attacks the queen and the bishop, and only the f-pawn can take it; declining is worse. Afterwards the e-pawns are isolated, the next knight move hits a loose bishop, and Black's kingside is slow. The engine still has Black about a pawn and a half ahead: a practical weapon, not a sound opening.
